title: UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC
description: Image source, GettyImage caption, A strategic military base is located on the Chagos archipelago's largest island, Diego GarciaByEwan SomervillePoliti
body: Image source, GettyImage caption, A strategic military base is located on the Chagos archipelago's largest island, Diego GarciaByEwan SomervillePolitical reporterUpdated 26 minutes agoThe UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being looked at again after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.In April the deal, agreed under Sir Keir Starmer, was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it"."What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing," he told BBC Breakfast."So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it."Streeting said the focus now would be to secure a long-term certainty for the base on Diego Garcia, the Chagos archipelago's largest island.He said it had been the view of every UK prime minister since Boris Johnson that an ongoing legal process - as Mauritius argues it was illegally forced to give away the islands in 1965 to gain independence - risks the security of the base.During Trump's first face-to-face meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the UN General Assembly in New York, the US president criticised the "terrible deal" and said the UK was "going to be looking" at it.Burnham replied: "Yep."He later told broadcasters he has "inherited the situation and we need a resolution".Burnham added: "It's critical to safeguard the future of the base, and that matters to us for security reasons, but also clearly to the United States as well."What I said in the meeting is that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides, and we'll work hard to find it."The prime minister had spoken to his Mauritian counterpart, Navin Ramgoolam, ahead of his trip to New York.An official readout from that meeting said Burnham "reiterated his commitment to continue doing everything possible" along with the US to ratify the deal.Prior to the pause in April, the UK and Mauritius had signed an agreement in May 2025 but a final draft of the bill to hand over sovereignty of the islands had not passed Parliament.Under the terms of the deal agreed in 2025, Britain would hand sovereignty over the Indian Ocean archipelago to Mauritius but lease back the Diego Garcia base for 99 years, with official figures giving the total as £3.4bn.However, Sir Keir, who was then prime minister, came under heavy criticism from opponents who said the real cost of the deal could amount to about £35bn, adjusting for inflation, and risked allowing China to establish a presence on the archipelago.Trump has been a frequent critic of the deal, previously branding it a "a blight on our great ally" and an "act of total weakness".Reacting to the review, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called on Burnham to "just scrap this terrible deal".Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "The Chagos deal is dead. Thank God."Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday that no money would be handed over to Mauritius "at this stage" while officials review the deal.Describing the Diego Garcia base as "one of the most sensitive and valuable national security assets", he said work was underway to find a deal "that maybe not everyone loves, but everyone can live with".

schema.headline: UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC

title: Chris Mason: From inside the room, how Burnham survived first Trump meeting
description: As I crouched between the cameras, determined to catch Donald Trump's eye and ask a question, I listened to a president seeking to be magnanimous.Reme
body: As I crouched between the cameras, determined to catch Donald Trump's eye and ask a question, I listened to a president seeking to be magnanimous.Remember, Trump can and does do warmth when he wants to, as well as acerbic.Prime Minister Andy Burnham, a mayor a matter of months ago, sat next to the most powerful man in the world.Put like that, it sounds believable when he said in advance he was looking forward to the meeting, but there must have been a jab of nerves too.Burnham did look a little nervous as us reporters trooped into the room, but then, for the most part, the compliments flowed from the president.The original plan was for journalists to be invited in at the beginning of the meeting, perhaps just minutes after the men had first met.Instead, we were kept waiting while the private talks took place, which came with the upside that they had more to say about each other and what they had discussed than would otherwise have been the case.Burnham knew, the world knows, how explosive these rolling, free wheeling, live on camera encounters with Trump can go.It is rollercoaster without a harness stuff.Having got myself into the president's eyeline, I waited for the last syllable of Burnham's final word at the end of his opening remarks and I filled the brief silence with a question.Was the prime minister a man you can do business with, I asked the president, given your political differences?"I do, I think he's a natural business person. We've had a lot of discussions even before this meeting. We've spoken to each other numerous times on the phone. Yeah, I think so, I think so. He gets it. He understands what he has to do."The warmth was self evident. Perhaps the Downing Street nerves will have eased a bit.But how long would the questions keep going? This is the president's theatre and he decides how long the public performance lasts. On occasion they are way north of half an hour.This was a meeting on neutral territory, a windowless, nondescript meeting room down a dingy corridor in the basement of the United Nations. This wasn't the Oval Office of the White House. Perhaps that dialled down the sense of occasion a notch.Nonetheless, for how long could the president maintain the bonhomie and sense of agreement? A question about immigration, potentially a point of friction, came and went without incident. So too did the Burnham government's decision, announced by the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who was in the room, to sanction settlements in the West Bank, a decision which infuriated Israel. But on the future of the Chagos islands, the president couldn't hide his view that Britain's decision to cede sovereignty of them to Mauritius and then rent back the military base on Diego Garcia was "terrible."The president added: "I think the prime minister is going to be looking at [the deal]" and Burnham replied "yep".Ah, interesting.Later, it was my turn to do a short interview with the prime minister on behalf of all of the broadcasters.Burnham emphasised that the meeting was "very encouraging" and "we've established a good connection."But what about the Chagos deal? Would it change, I asked. Pointedly, he described it as a deal he had "inherited"."We've got to find a resolution, and so work will continue now…to see where that resolution might lead."In other words, it looks like it is going to change.Flashpoints down the track with Trump are near inevitable — barely any leader avoids them with this administration, and Burnham may want to lean into some, in time.And even those he doesn't might lean into him, Chagos possibly one of them.But outwardly Burnham has a relationship with the president he can now build on after this opening face to face conversation.What followed in the prime minister's remaining meetings at the UN were diplomacy by convention, not the wild ride with Trump he had just stepped off and survived.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: From inside the room, how Burnham survived first Trump meeting

title: UK to fight Russian disinformation and push new global AI standards, Burnham says
description: The UK will set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of disinformation, including from Russia, and lead efforts to establish global safety sta
body: The UK will set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of disinformation, including from Russia, and lead efforts to establish global safety standards for artificial intelligence, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.In his first major international speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City, Burnham warned Russian agencies are using "every means at their disposal", including bots and fake websites, to "spread lies and disinformation". The prime minister noted AI will "multiply" existing threats, and pitched the UK as an "honest broker" on the technology.Fears about AI have grown after industry insiders recently warned it could threaten humanity.In Burnham's speech, he accused Russia of running a disinformation campaign."The Kremlin spends around £1.3bn each year on manipulating information," Burnham told the UN General Assembly."They've used bots and fake websites, falsified newspaper articles, forged the branding of 28 British organisations, including universities and the BBC."We're talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people's homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair. "On top of that we have seen cyber-attacks on our companies and institutions. And we know that AI will multiply the threat."'He also referenced the 2019 UK general election, in which the government previously said Russia almost certainly sought to interfere.To counter this, Burnham announced a new National Centre for Information Defence to detect and disrupt AI-enabled disinformation campaigns by hostile states.The centre will work alongside intelligence agencies, government departments, law enforcement and social media to bring together expertise to combat "information warfare".There was no immediate comment from Russia, a representative of which was sitting in the room listening to Burnham. When the UK government put out a report in 2020 about Russian activity in the UK, including in elections, Moscow described the allegations as "Russophobia".Addressing a forum about disinformation in Moscow on Tuesday, before the prime minister's speech, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused Western media of embracing "anti-Russian cliches and fantasies".Before becoming prime minister, Burnham had said relatively little about how AI should be regulated.Since taking power in July, Burnham's government has stressed the need for international cooperation to combat the risks, as well as harness the potential benefits of the technology, warning that further regulation and legislation may be needed.In his speech, Burnham described the most advanced "Frontier AI" as "one of the most significant challenges and opportunities of our age".He told world leaders AI would be "key to economic growth" but also a "multiplier of risk".The prime minister added: "We've all heard the warnings – which we must heed. I know how worried people are. So we have to rise to this moment."Burnham said the "UK has a unique position as an honest broker", with close ties to the US and the European Union.He also highlighted the UK's "world-leading" AI Security Institute,  which was established under Conservative Prime Minister Rishi Sunak and tests major AI models to improve their safety before they are released publicly.He pledged to put AI "at the heart of the UK's G20 Presidency next year", when leaders of the world's biggest economies will gather in Manchester.Burnham said the UK would work towards agreeing a set of global principles and standards to ensure transparency, access to AI models, and that development happens safely.He added that this would "bring together welcome initiatives from others", such as a proposal from Norway this week.The declaration - which has the support of more than 20 countries, including Germany, Canada and Ireland - calls for AI to remain under human control and for mandatory pre-release testing of frontier models.However, it has not been signed by the US and China, which dominate AI development, or the UK.Former cabinet minister Darren Jones, who served as chief secretary to Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, called on the prime minister to sign the declaration and offer to broker an agreement with the US on its implementation.He argued there "should be a landing zone to agree mandatory testing", without undermining competitive advantage between companies and nations.The UK AI Security Institute's testing of models is currently on a voluntary basis and AI company Anthropic reportedly refused to submit its latest model for testing.Downing Street said officials had made clear in recent discussions with AI leaders that the government expects "full and total visibility of model developments".The prime minister has acknowledged that while developers have made significant commitments on transparency, nothing is off the table to keep the public safe, including legislation.Meanwhile, the government has announced a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.

schema.headline: UK to fight Russian disinformation and push new global AI standards, Burnham says

title: Drug deaths rise sharply in Scotland as figures remain worst in Europe
description: ByScotland editorUpdated 9 minutes agoDeaths related to illicit drugs rose by 11% in Scotland last year to 1,133 as the country struggles to tackle th
body: ByScotland editorUpdated 9 minutes agoDeaths related to illicit drugs rose by 11% in Scotland last year to 1,133 as the country struggles to tackle the worst fatality rate in Europe.National Records of Scotland (NRS) said the figure for 2025 was 116 higher than the previous year, bringing the total deaths in a decade to more than 11,000.After adjusting for age, there were 21.4 drug-related deaths per million people.NRS defines drug-related deaths as those where the underlying cause was drug poisoning, a controlled substance was in the body at the time of death, and drug use led directly to the death.Efforts to save lives over the past year have been hampered by criminal gangs mixing powerful synthetic opioids such as nitazenes with existing drugs including heroin, cocaine and fake Valium pills. NRS said the increase had been driven by a rise in deaths of male drug users. This increased by 19%, while the rate of female deaths fell by 5%.The rate of drug-related deaths in the most deprived areas of Scotland was 15 times as high as in the least deprived areas.The average age of death has increased from 32 in 2000 to 46 years in 2025.When comparing Scotland with the rest of Europe, NRS measures the death rate among 15-64 year olds - which was 277 per million in 2025.The next highest rate in Europe was Estonia with 112 deaths per million in 2024, the most recent year for which figures are available from the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA).Scotland's death rate in 2024 was 246 per million.NRS says its methodology produces "similar" outcomes to EUDA's count of "drug-induced deaths", with the caveat that the two methods use slightly different lists of drugs.When comparing Scotland with the rest of the UK, NRS uses a wider measure of age-adjusted drug poisoning deaths.This includes all deaths where the underlying cause was listed as mental and behavioural disorders due to psychoactive substance abuse or poisoning by drugs whether accidental, intentional, of unknown intent or as a result of assault.The most recent comparable data are for 2024 and show that Scotland had an age-adjusted death rate of 216 per million compared with 91 for England, 140 for Wales and 135 for Northern Ireland.This breaking news story is being updated and more details will be published shortly. Please refresh the page for the fullest version.You can receive Breaking News on a smartphone or tablet via the BBC News App. You can also follow @BBCBreaking on X, external to get the latest alerts.

schema.headline: Drug deaths rise sharply in Scotland as figures remain worst in Europe

title: Trump administration accuses banned media outlets of 'falsehoods' ahead of court hearing
description: The US Justice Department has filed documents that accuse three media outlets banned from the White House of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods" an
body: The US Justice Department has filed documents that accuse three media outlets banned from the White House of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods" and reporting which "threatened national security" as it prepared to defend the move in court.Last week, President Donald Trump barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news".After their reporters had their passes confiscated and were denied access to the building, the three outlets jointly launched legal action, calling the move unconstitutional.On Wednesday, a judge is set to decide whether to issue an order temporarily lifting the ban, pending a full hearing.According to a court filing by the Justice Department in a District of Columbia court, the three outlets were issued with a list of "reporting incidents" by the White House ahead of the ban.The filing cites a number of stories about construction at the White House - including about a security bunker and the building of a new ballroom, as well as a report on an internal information leak investigation. It goes on to say that "access to the White House is a privilege, not a right".The three media organisations have argued that the ban breaches their rights under the First Amendment, which forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press.In a joint statement confirming legal action against the government, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting."Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."Major TV networks have withdrawn from a media-sharing arrangement of video and images of the president, known as the pool, in protest over the ban.Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president.

schema.headline: Trump administration accuses banned media outlets of 'falsehoods' ahead of court hearing

title: Nigella Lawson is 'brilliant addition' to The Great British Bake Off, TV critics say
description: Nigella Lawson is 'icing on the cake', TV critics say as she enters Bake Off tentImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Nigella has taken over from Prue
body: Nigella Lawson is 'icing on the cake', TV critics say as she enters Bake Off tentImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Nigella has taken over from Prue Leith as a judge on Bake Off alongside Paul HollywoodBySteven McIntoshEntertainment reporter TV critics have described Nigella Lawson as the "icing on the cake" of The Great British Bake Off, as the show returned for a new series on Tuesday.Lawson has replaced Dame Prue Leith, who announced she was leaving earlier this year after nearly a decade in the programme's famous tent.The Telegraph said Lawson gives the Channel 4 series a "new lease of life", while Digital Spy agreed she was a "brilliant addition" to the line-up.But the Independent was cooler on the launch episode as a whole, saying the show "wastes Nigella's prodigious charms and misses chance for a true revamp".The return of Bake Off saw Lawson join fellow judge Paul Hollywood, who has appeared on the programme since its launch in 2010, and presenters Alison Hammond and Noel Fielding. Former Bake Off winner Giuseppe Dell'Anno told BBC Radio 4's Today that Lawson "did produce a step change" to the show and was a "nice fit with the ethos of the programme"."She was doing her best by capturing the vibes of a cake, the feelings, what it makes you think of, which was very nicely balanced by Paul being very technical and scrutinising," he said."I think, however, that she will get better over time, because my gut feeling yesterday was that she was still in new territory."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Some critics noted Lawson did not deliver as much innuendo as expected during her first episodeIn a five-star review, the Guardian's Lucy Mangan, external said Lawson "moves through Bake Off dispensing words of wisdom, generous praise and gentle criticism".She added that Lawson is "just as confident as Leith but a much quieter, more soothing presence that works perfectly with Alison Hammond's ebullience and Paul Hollywood's teacher-ish vibe".The Telegraph's Anita Singh, external also awarded five stars, remarking that "Bake Off and Nigella are a match made in heaven"."She brings glamour, intelligence and poise. And, of course, a hefty dollop of innuendo," Singh said."Lawson is supportive in her judging but not afraid to tell the bakers where they can improve. She gives helpful advice."The launch episode was described as "one of the most disastrous openers ever" by Metro's Adam Miller, external - but luckily he was only referring to the cakes."When Bake Off should be crumbling after 17 seasons, Nigella Lawson is making Channel 4's crown jewel fresher than ever," he said."It's clear to see she is the lifeline Bake Off needed to ensure it could easily have another decade or more in it yet."'Stale format'However, other critics said Channel 4 had missed an opportunity to revitalise the programme.Awarding two stars, the Independent's Nick Hilton, external said Lawson quickly "feels part of the fabric," adding: "But this is also the problem. The Bake Off format is very tired."He wrote: "The cakes wobble, the decorations melt, the bakers over-salt the batter, and everything remains the same."Nigella's arrival might have been an opportunity for a harder refresh. But instead of bending the format to suit Nigella, the new judge bends to the will of the programme."Hilton acknowledged that producers "might have done brilliantly to snag Nigella, and it will undoubtedly lead to an uptick in viewers". "But they've applied her prodigious charms too thinly, and even she – with her preference for all things 'sumptuous' – can't stop the feeling that the show has gone more than a little stale."Several critics noted that Lawson did not deliver as much innuendo as expected during her debut in the tent."Add Nigella – famous for her on-screen coquettish eyelash-fluttering and cheeky language choices – into the mix, and you'd imagine the sauciness gets dialled up to 11,"  said the Radio Times's Jane Rackham, external."Instead, she's cut back on the sauce. She makes well-informed and helpful comments about the amateur bakers' efforts."Digital Spy's Janet A Leigh agreed, external, noting: "As is the nature of Bake Off, there were many opportunities for Nigella to engage with the playful, flirtatious nature that has underpinned the show since its inception. Yet every opportunity was gently rebuffed."Instead, she said, Lawson "has a way of talking about food that celebrates it and expands the audience's understanding of flavours without seeming pretentious."If episode one is just a flavour of what to expect from Nigella, then it is hugely encouraging. She cares deeply, steers wisely, and slots effortlessly into the close-knit team." Image source, PA MediaWhen Lawson was faced with innuendo-laden comments from contestants or co-stars, she often "wisely said nothing", noted the Daily Mail's Jan Moir., external"Ultimately this was a tremendous debut performance from the new mistress of meringue, showing a side of Nigella we have not seen before: quirky, commanding, funny – but also humane," she concluded.Ben Dowell of the Times observed, external: "Bake Off has always been one of TV's more beguiling offerings with a comforting romance about it. "It's not perfect. Hammond is ebullience and warmth personified but her co-presenter, the erstwhile Mighty Boosh comedian Fielding, still looks a bit lost, as if he has wandered in from the wrong set."But with Nigella the show is definitely in safe hands. Bake Off has found a new star."

schema.headline: Nigella Lawson is 'brilliant addition' to The Great British Bake Off, TV critics say

title: Open wounds and eyes that can't close - women warn about cheap bleph eyelid surgery
description: They have told the BBC the demand for this procedure, which normally costs thousands of pounds in the UK, has increased as part of a wider aesthetic t
body: They have told the BBC the demand for this procedure, which normally costs thousands of pounds in the UK, has increased as part of a wider aesthetic trend to tighten, smooth and lift the face.Surgeons say complications have been linked to clinics across mainland Europe, Africa and Asia, and, when they occur, the lack of aftercare puts a burden on the NHS.As well as Nikita, we have spoken to dozens of people who have experienced problems - including one woman who had to tape her eyes shut to sleep because too much eyelid skin had been removed, while another feared she was losing her sight. UK surgeons have also told us they have seen patients unable to close their eyes properly after treatment abroad. Nikita, from Dublin, wanted to make her eyes more defined, but could not afford upper eyelid surgery in Ireland that she was told would cost more than €4,000 (£3,400).Then the 31-year-old discovered on TikTok that she could get a bleph with Dutch company, Faceland for €750 (£650).She described its clinic in Düsseldorf as "like a conveyor belt, just one in, one out constantly".The company says it has performed more than 2,950 bleph procedures on UK patients at its clinics in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland since October 2024.It says it offers "safe and quality" treatments and told us "less than 1% of procedures have led to a complaint", although this does not include everyone who needed revision surgery.The majority of patients who spoke to the BBC about problems with their blephs had been to the company's clinics - but we do not know how many complications in total have occurred at Faceland.Nikita, who went for her bleph in November 2025, says she did not realise how invasive the procedure would be, believing it to be like "getting your lips or Botox done", she says.She was injected with local anaesthetic, but when the doctor began cutting delicate eyelid skin, she felt pain she had never experienced before."I went into shell shock, it was horrible," Nikita says. "When she was stitching me I could feel the needle going through my skin."In the past three years, videos about blephs posted by UK social media accounts on four leading platforms were viewed nearly 150 million times, BBC analysis has found. This figure is five times greater than the previous three years.Many people report positive results in their posts, and a lot have been treated at Faceland.One woman told us her droopy eyelids had been restricting her vision and causing her headaches. She was not eligible for NHS treatment and could not afford to go private in the UK, but now she says, after going to Faceland, her issues have been resolved.The company's website claims it is changing the market by focusing on "affordable, accessible and high quality care". Treatments are carried out by accredited medical doctors who receive internal training by Faceland in surgical procedures, it says.Surgeons in the UK told us upper eyelid surgery typically takes about three hours, including preparation, surgery and post-operation care. But Faceland patients we have spoken to say they spent less than an hour at the clinics.Faceland says allowing practitioners to perform a higher volume of treatments helps significantly lower costs.Eight days after her Faceland bleph surgery, Laura, not her real name, made her first of four visits to A&E because her eyelid wounds had reopened.Her procedure at the company's Amsterdam clinic in June had seemingly gone smoothly, but problems began when she took her stitches out back home in the UK, something many patients do when they have treatment abroad.The crescent shaped cuts above her eyes which had been held together by the stitches came apart, exposing raw, red wounds which became infected. This should hardly ever happen if a practitioner has been properly trained, UK surgeons told us.The first time this happened, Laura, who is in her early 40s, says she called Faceland's emergency helpline several times, but could not get through. Desperate, she rushed to A&E."When I closed my eyes for too long the tension would cause my wounds to open up again," she says. "I was scared to go to sleep and was in constant agony."The BBC has seen emails that show Caryn contacted Faceland twice, to report what had happened, and that she received a short reply 12 days later. A few further emails followed, but Caryn says she has not heard from the company since.Faceland maintains it "did not leave her without support or follow-up during the aftercare process".It says it is sorry if patients felt insufficiently supported by its teams or experienced complications.Like Caryn, Laura and Nikita, patients we have spoken to who have had cheap eyelid surgery abroad say limited aftercare is their biggest complaint."Aftercare for the typical bleph should be available to a patient 24/7," says Vize. "If your surgeon is hundreds of miles away, the ability to provide care with a sense of immediacy is impossible."He also warns that patients should be aware that in some cases lower costs may mean lower standards.The company also says patients can come back to a Faceland clinic to have stitches removed, but no-one we spoke to had done that.Patients removing their own stitches is "a recipe for disaster", according to Vize, who says stitches should be taken out by a surgeon or a nurse to reduce the infection risk and the chance of wounds splitting open.Nikita is mostly happy with her results, aside from a small scar, but she wants other people to learn from her experiences and fully understand the risks."If I'd had the money or if I hadn't listened to the spin on TikTok, I probably would have gone somewhere closer to home and not rushed into it," she says.Nearly two years on, Caryn still has issues with her left eye, including some blurry vision and scarring.Meanwhile, Laura fears she may have scars above both of her eyes for life."I tried to fix a problem that didn't really need fixing, and I've come back with a bigger problem that I need surgery for, and I can't afford that," she says. "It's pretty devastating."

schema.headline: Open wounds and eyes that can't close - women warn about cheap bleph eyelid surgery

title: Hurricane Polo intensifies into rare category 5 storm off the coast of Mexico
description: Hurricane Polo has rapidly intensified off the coast of Mexico to become one of the most powerful storms of the season in the Pacific Ocean.A Hurrican
body: Hurricane Polo has rapidly intensified off the coast of Mexico to become one of the most powerful storms of the season in the Pacific Ocean.A Hurricane Hunter aircraft, operated by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), flew into the storm on Tuesday and recorded sustained wind speeds near 180 mph (285 km/h), with stronger gusts.NOAA's Miami-based National Hurricane Center called the storm "extremely dangerous" and said its intensification over 24 hours was "truly remarkable".The slow-moving storm is fuelling up on extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon and is the season's third category 5 storm, the highest level on the Saffir-Simpson scale.The storm is predicted to skirt the coast of south-western Mexico, but is not expected to make landfall, a warning from NOAA said.As it slowly drifts northwest, Polo will drive torrential rainfall in parts of Mexico's south-west coast - which could lead to deadly flooding and mudslides, NOAA said.Rainfall totals of up to 6in (15cm) are forecast, with 8in possible in some areas. Residents have also been warned of large ocean swells and life-threatening surf conditions for the next few days."So far, the information we have is that (Polo) will not make a direct landfall on the coast," Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Tuesday, but she warned residents along the Pacific coast to be vigilant. Sheinbaum highlighted the states of Jalisco, Colima and Michoacan as being at risk. Data from the Hurricane Hunter aircraft indicated that Polo could still strengthen and would likely stay a category 5 storm for the next few days, because of what NOAA called a "very conducive" environment of extremely warm ocean waters feeding the storm.

schema.headline: Hurricane Polo intensifies into rare category 5 storm off the coast of Mexico

title: South Africa mass shooting: Gunmen kill 11 at house in Durban
description: At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting in a residential building near the South African city of Durban.Gunmen stormed a house in the K
body: At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting in a residential building near the South African city of Durban.Gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township late on Tuesday and opened fire on 14 people. Ten were killed at the scene and four were taken to hospital, where one later died from their injuries, police said.Police said some of the victims were on their watch in connection with illegal activities, which they could not "divulge at the moment to protect investigations which have been launched".While the motive of the shooting has not yet confirmed, the police said they could not rule out a "feud between rival groupings". "Information available at this stage suggests that 13 men and one woman, who is believed to be pregnant, were reportedly having a party inside a house when three men arrived and opened fire on them," the police said in a statement. The woman is among those who died.A local TV reporter from the eNCA channel at the scene said the gunmen had set fire to a vehicle belonging to one of the victims before fleeing, with footage showing the burnt-out car.The police say they have launched a manhunt for the suspects.South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, with police data showing a murder rate equivalent to more than 60 deaths a day.In recent weeks, the gruesome discovery of at least nine murdered women, with some of the bodies dumped by the roadside, has heightened fears in the country.Last year, nine people were killed in a mass shooting at a tavern in Johannesburg.Rivalry among criminal gangs amid turf wars, drug trafficking and illegal mining is common in the country, often driving violence within communities.In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa said organised crime was "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development", as he announced that he would be deploying the army to support the police.

schema.headline: South Africa mass shooting: Gunmen kill 11 at house in Durban

title: UK and US warned to take action on spiralling debt costs by IMF
description: The world's advanced economies including the UK and US need to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels following weeks of spiralling government interest
body: The world's advanced economies including the UK and US need to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels following weeks of spiralling government interest costs, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.In an exclusive interview, Kristalina Georgieva said global economic shocks had been "pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven" but that governments had taken "no action to contain that service cost"."[It's] time to take that action," she said, adding that "courage" was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.The intervention comes as government borrowing costs have surged in response to wars disrupting the supply of oil, which has fuelled inflation.Higher global borrowing costs have hit the UK government in the run-up to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first Budget next month, with speculation building over potential tax and spending policies.The latest figures show borrowing - the difference between tax receipts and government spending - was £18.3bn ($24.4bn) in August, almost a fifth higher than the year before and higher than official forecasts. Meanwhile, debt interest was the highest figure for August since monthly records began in 1997.Higher borrowing costs have also hit the US, the world's largest economy, which has seen its debt pile surpass $40tn. The amount has doubled within the space of a decade, prompting concerns at home and abroad.On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Georgieva said the IMF's message to advanced economies was that while there were economic factors occurring outside the control of governments, they did have command over domestic policies."There are these two things that must be done: bring debt levels down, put fiscal consolidation as a priority, and make sure that the central banks deliver on their mandate for price stability," she said."It is impossible to stress strongly enough how critical it is to get the courage to take the steps that are necessary. These are politically tough steps to take, but necessary steps to take."Asked specifically about the UK's higher interest costs compared to other major economies, Georgieva said its position was "not very different" from others. She pointed to "fairly consistent action" on lowering debt and praised planning and housing reforms, adding that advanced economies "don't have the cash" to boost growth and so had to rely on reforms to encourage the private sector to invest.Governments around the world raise money by selling bonds - essentially an IOU - and in return pay interest to the investment funds that buy them.Concerns over inflation eating away at returns has sent the interest rates on bonds - known as yields - higher in recent months. But there are other factors pushing yields up, including increasing competition in the bond market from large tech companies looking to raise huge amounts of money to invest in artificial intelligence (AI) development.On AI, Georgieva referenced recent concerns about loss of safe control over such systems as a potential financial stability problem, alongside debt levels."If we see more incidents when AI takes [on a] life of its own, then we can be faced with a significant financial stability risk," she said.The IMF's managing director repeated the influential body's assessment that the global economy was affected by two forces "pushing in opposite directions" - the energy price shock and investment in AI.She said it was important for the low exports of oil and gas from the Gulf "to resume in a durable manner, for the energy supply shock to finally be in the rearview mirror"."That is a very significant step to normalisation," she said, but acknowledged it was yet to happen.

schema.headline: UK and US warned to take action on spiralling debt costs by IMF

title: England vs Sri Lanka: Will Jacks' career-best 5-22 helps hosts win in Durham
description: First Metro Bank one-day international, Chester-le-StreetEngland 265 (48.1 overs): Brook 67 (69); Colombage 3-44 Sri Lanka 176 (37 overs): Wellalage 4
body: First Metro Bank one-day international, Chester-le-StreetEngland 265 (48.1 overs): Brook 67 (69); Colombage 3-44 Sri Lanka 176 (37 overs): Wellalage 45 (36); Jacks 5-22England won by 89 runsScorecardWill Jacks' all-round efforts helped England grind out an 89-run victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international at Chester-le-Street to continue their quiet revival in white-ball cricket. Faced with a slow and low pitch, Jacks made 46 not out after 67 from Harry Brook and 44 from Joe Root, meaning England posted 265 despite being bowled out in 48.1 overs.That score appeared only par but a professional bowling performance limited Sri Lanka's scoring and found regular wickets.Jacks took the big wickets of Kusal Mendis and Charith Asalanka and then wrapped up the tail for career-best figures of 5-22. Sri Lanka, much improved in the field but far too timid with the bat, were bowled out for 176.England, who have now won 10 white-ball matches in a row against Sri Lanka this year, can seal a third ODI series win in a row with a game to spare on Thursday at Headingley. The three-match contest concludes on Sunday at The Oval - a match that brings down the curtain on one of the most topsy-turvy summers in recent memory.This was not vintage England. For the first time since 2019 they did not hit a six batting first.Captain Brook and coach Brendon McCullum should not mind that, however. For too long, England have only been able to win when piling up big scores.Yes, they were dismissed for the 12th time since McCullum took charge of the white-ball sides last year and, as so often this summer, the quality of the opposition can be questioned.But Brook was the only batter to fall in a middle order collapse of 4-29 playing an aggressive shot. He sliced a drive to deep cover after batting in a restrained manner, while Sri Lanka's debutant leg-spinner Sachindu Colombage, who found a hint of turn to hit Root's off stump, had Jos Buttler lbw for 31 and bowled Overton with a googly for eight, was impressive.After the collapse, Jacks could have swung hard but batted responsibly to stretch out the innings from 211-7 in the 39th over.He took 18 runs from the 47th over and was primed to cut loose before Asitha Fernando, having dismissed opener Tom Banton for 10 with a bail-trimmer in the powerplay, found reverse swing to bowl Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue. Jacks' importance to England's white-ball sides is growing with every match.They will need bigger scores by the time the World Cup comes around in a year's time but, after beating Sri Lanka at the start of the year and toppling India in July, they are now primed to enter two months of white-ball cricket overseas on the back of another series win.With Adil Rashid out of this series with a hand injury, much of the attention was on Rehan Ahmed, who has a rare chance to press his case as England's leg-spinner.After being carelessly run-out for two, he dropped a caught-and-bowled chance in his first over and conceded 46 runs in seven overs. Those figures were harsh but he will hope for better before the series is out.Instead, it was Jacks who played the lead spinner's role with his off-spin, barely bowling a bad ball.Asalanka and Mendis were pinned attempting sweeps and Dunith Wellalage, who hit two sixes in a 36-ball 45 at number seven, was tempted to sky a catch to mid-on. When Fernando and Dilshan Madushanka followed, Jacks had the best figures by an England spinner since Vic Marks in 1984.England's total was also the lowest they have defended in a full ODI since July 2022 – before their dismal 2023 World Cup or their winless run at last year's Champions Trophy.Gus Atkinson bowled well for 1-25 in seven overs and Jamie Overton 2-21 in five. The seamers all bowled hard lengths and were rewarded.

schema.headline: England vs Sri Lanka: Will Jacks' career-best 5-22 helps hosts win in Durham

title: Fresh bedsheets and dusk walks: Experts' sleep tips for freshers
description: Image source, Anna-May DixonImage caption, Twenty-year-old Anna-May manages on about five hours' sleep a nightByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterIt's the
body: Image source, Anna-May DixonImage caption, Twenty-year-old Anna-May manages on about five hours' sleep a nightByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterIt's the start of university - you're already on your fourth themed night out of the week and have signed up for every quirky-sounding society your campus has to offer. But your relationship with your bed could be key to keeping up with a busy social life, as well as that lengthy reading list."If you can get out before 11am-ish then there's a part of the brain, just behind the eyes, that responds to light," says Jo Baker, a psychotherapist and student sleep and mental health expert."Getting daylight early on in the day is really going to help to keep your body in check. How you sleep at night starts with how you wake up in the morning."Sleep is essential to learning and absorbing information. But late nights out, noisy flatmates and a strange new bed can mean good sleep habits go out the window.Image source, Anna-May DixonImage caption, She tries to stay awake during her commute to uni but admits sometimes "dosing off a bit"For Anna-May, 20, it's her four-hour round trip from Kendal, Cumbria to study dance at the University of Salford that leaves her short of sleep. She gets about five hours a night - the alarm goes at 05:00."I track my sleep and get worried about how little I will get, and then sometimes that keeps me up," she says. "I can tell I'm more tired towards the end of the week and things can feel harder."Forcing yourself to have an early night isn't going to work, according to Baker, especially if you end up lying wide awake in bed."Your brain learns this is somewhere I lie and get stressed about not being able to sleep - so the most important thing is a consistent waking time," she says.Alcohol and caffeine don't helpWhen you feel groggy, it's tempting to chug multiple coffees or fizzy drinks. But caffeine hangs around in the body and blocks the build-up of sleepiness throughout the day. Too many flat whites and you'll not only be short of cash - you could also develop a sleep problem.Alcohol may also be a tempting way to boost your confidence around new people, but it doesn't help you sleep. "When you fall asleep [after large amounts of alcohol], you're anaesthetised really. It's like having an anaesthetic. You're not asleep," Baker says.In fact, alcohol pushes out the deep sleep which restores you physically, and replaces it with lighter sleep, which doesn't.Emma Young, deputy director of student services for health and wellbeing at Manchester Metropolitan University points out the low-key alternatives during freshers' week."There are lots of alcohol-free events now, like sip and paint. You can also try wellness and wellbeing clubs, like yoga and crafts, if you don't fancy the sport or music societies."Switch off properly before sleepAnna-May likes a hot shower or bath before bed, which research suggests helps the body's core temperature to cool down and prepare for sleep.Then the only way she can get to sleep is to watch episodes of Friends on her iPad."I watch something I have seen time and time again - it's enough to quieten the busy part of my mind and I can fall to sleep," she says.Image source, Elly WelfordImage caption, Anna-May, who is studying dance, accepts that watching TV before bed goes "against all the advice"But activities without screens like journalling or reading a book might be best for creating a calm, gradual transition to sleep. Listening to music or a podcast can also work.The natural hormone melatonin rises before bedtime, making us feel sleepy. But watching social media reels or films means your eyes stay active, blocking that process and keeping you awake.Baker also suggests: Switching off screens an hour and a half before bed Avoiding a heavy meal just before going to bedWashing your sheets so they are nice and clean to get intoChucking a throw over your laptop, books and desk so you know work is done for the dayGoing for a walk at dusk - the changing light is a signal to the brainKeeping your bed for sleeping in (rather than eating, working or watching YouTube)Image source, Joanna BakerImage caption, Student sleep expert Jo Baker says making your bed in the morning can help signal that sleep is overPlan for feeling ill in bedFeeling unwell can of course impact your sleep patterns.Freshers' flu is tricky to avoid, but good hand hygiene - washing regularly or using antibacterial hand gel - might just reduce your chances of getting a fever, sore throat and blocked nose, and spending a day or two in bed.Meningitis is far more dangerous and requires urgent medical help (call 999). It can look a lot like freshers' flu but if it's not diagnosed, it can progress very quickly and lead to seizures, brain damage and sepsis. That's why a free NHS vaccine called Men B is now on offer to all freshers students.Many universities recommend planning ahead in case you feel ill and need some medical help at some point, especially if you're living away from home.A typical to-do list should include:Registering with a local GPFinding your nearest chemistRegistering with an NHS dentistFinding out where the closest A&E isYou might also want to check out what your uni has to offer in terms of mental health support. Some pair up students for peer support and run dedicated 24-hour phone lines.Websites like Student Minds, external have lots of useful advice and information.And if you're not feeling like yourself, Young suggests a regular call home, to family or a best friend.

schema.headline: Fresh bedsheets and dusk walks: Experts' sleep tips for freshers

title: Emma Raducanu inspired by Andre Agassi in plotting route back to top of tennis
description: As Emma Raducanu plots a route back to the pinnacle of tennis, the Briton has been taking inspiration from Andre Agassi's 2009 autobiography.Five year
body: As Emma Raducanu plots a route back to the pinnacle of tennis, the Briton has been taking inspiration from Andre Agassi's 2009 autobiography.Five years have passed since Raducanu's remarkable US Open triumph, when at the age of 18 she became the first qualifier in the Open era to win a Grand Slam.American Agassi was a teenage prodigy himself and later claimed the first of his eight major singles titles at Wimbledon in 1992 aged 22.But between the peak years of his career, he had to overcome a challenging period when he went four years without a major and dropped to 141st in the world rankings."I was especially intrigued by the passage where he got out of his slump in the late 1990s by creating his own training regimen and finding his way back to the top," Raducanu told Uniqlo."It speaks in depth about his early successes and the lows he reached, perhaps as a result of them."A lot of it was so relatable."Agassi said his hope was for his experiences to help other players going through similar periods in their own careers."It's wonderful to hear that anybody can relate," Agassi told BBC Breakfast."It was literally the hope that if one person read it and it gave them hope, some tools to understand that they're not alone, they can figure it out and get to a healthier place without having to direct their frustrations at the game of tennis, then it was a success for me."So, hearing that 17 years later it can still impact somebody, especially in this game, it does make me feel good."Raducanu reached a career-high ranking of 10 in July 2022, but the 23-year-old has slipped to 98th in the world.Her progress continues to be hampered by physical issues, and she most recently missed the US Open as she continues her recovery from a stress fracture in her lower right leg.A foot injury disrupted her pre-season training before she spent two-and-a-half months off court with a post-viral illness earlier this year.But Raducanu enjoyed one of the best weeks of her career at Queen's Club in June, reaching her biggest final since her triumph in New York five years ago.Agassi won all four of the sport's Grand Slams and claimed Olympic singles gold at the 1996 Games.Asked what advice he would give Raducanu, Agassi said: "I would encourage her to focus on being the best of herself on a daily basis, but don't judge that by results or thinking that somehow you have to be 100%."You have to learn to be 100% of whatever percent you're at [and] be comfortable in your own identity inside of that - not what people say."Back in my day, I could just put down the paper and not read it. Now it seems like it's harder for these youngsters to avoid."For Agassi, tennis was by no means a childhood passion. His father, keen for his son to become the very best, would introduce him to others as a future number one tennis player.That additional pressure, Agassi says, led him to play with "fear". It was not until he sank from world number one to 141st that he felt able to reconnect with the sport.Agassi, who created a foundation providing education for under-served children during that time, said: "I had more success from that point forward than I did playing out of fear."The first thing I would advise a parent to think about is that it's not their life, it's their child."You raise a child in their way and they'll never depart from it. You just have to find out what their way is."Agassi will captain Team USA in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London later this week, between 25-27 September."Tennis is a hamster wheel of sorts - the fact that these guys make room in their schedule to play this incredible event tells you how great this event is," Agassi added."We're obviously playing Team Europe, in Europe, so I don't know where the crowd is going to have their heart."But I know one thing - they're going to see some spectacular tennis."

schema.headline: Emma Raducanu inspired by Andre Agassi in plotting route back to top of tennis

title: Robbie Ure: From leaving Rangers to La Liga - Scotland is next step for striker
description: Robbie Ure, cool and confident and 22 years old, played 90 minutes for Sevilla against Barcelona at the weekend; 90 minutes of being marked by Pau Cub
body: Robbie Ure, cool and confident and 22 years old, played 90 minutes for Sevilla against Barcelona at the weekend; 90 minutes of being marked by Pau Cubarsi, man of the match in the World Cup final, 90 minutes of pitch-time with Rodri, player of the tournament, 90 minutes of breathing the same rarefied air as Lamine Yamal.Ure is a part of a new-ish wave of Scotland striker, uncapped but hopeful of making a debut on Saturday away to Slovenia in the Nations League. There is no Lyndon Dykes in Sebastien Pocognoli's squad and no George Hirst. Injury has ruled out Che Adams, Lawrence Shankland and Ross Stewart. Those five were all at the World Cup in the United States during the summer.Now, it's Ure alongside James Wilson of Hearts and Kieron Bowie of Sassuolo, who both have two caps, and Oli McBurnie of Hull, with the last of his 16 international appearances coming five years ago.There is an intriguing freshness to this and nowhere is that buzz more obvious than in the story of Ure, the boy who wanted to play for Rangers but couldn't force his way in, the young man who in his seven games for Sevilla since his move from IK Sirius in Sweden has already played against 12 of Spain's World Cup winning squad.Just over three years ago, Ure left Rangers as a teenager, his last forays with the senior team being one minute against St Mirren in November 2022 and another minute against Hibs in May 2023.Belgium was the first step on his road to the Scotland team but Sweden was when it all started to happen. In 2025-26, he scored 11 goals in 30 games, a mere warm-up for what was to follow. Between April and July this year, Ure played 14 games for IK Sirius and scored 15 goals, including four in one game against Mjallby."I was scoring near enough every game, so that was probably the happiest I've been," he says. "Every week I was scoring and we were top of the league. I was improving and that interest in me was getting bigger and bigger."At a young age it's really important you're playing. I was playing 90 minutes every week, getting trust from the manager and from the club. I was given time as well. The day I scored the four goals, it was my first hat-trick. I felt like every time I shot it was going to be a goal. I've not had a feeling like that before in football. It was pretty special."Player pathway is a hot topic in Scottish football and Ure is an example of what can happen when a kid is given a proper chance."Everyone's different," he says. "You have to give players patience and give them time to develop but the way to do that is, of course, playing minutes at a level where you can develop at. I couldn't find that level in Scotland, so I had to look elsewhere and I'm happy that I did that."The level he has found in Spain is stratospheric. No goals yet, but it's a savagely tough school. He will have his moment under Pocognoli in the coming weeks. Four games in quick succession - he will get his first cap and his first chance to shine on another stage. And he's earned it.

schema.headline: Robbie Ure: From leaving Rangers to La Liga - Scotland is next step for striker

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Burn to be mild' and 'Pulp fiction'
description: The prime minister's first encounter in-person with US President Donald Trump makes nearly all the front pages, with many focusing on the comments bet
body: The prime minister's first encounter in-person with US President Donald Trump makes nearly all the front pages, with many focusing on the comments between the two about the controversial Chagos Islands deal which would see the UK hand sovereignty of the islands to Mauritius. The Daily Mirror, external says Burnham "emerged with credit" after what it called a "tricky meeting", where Trump described the deal as "terrible". The i Paper, external described the meeting as "magnanimous". The Daily Telegrah's, external headline says "Burnham bows to Trump on Chagos" after the prime minister agreed to "review" the deal.The strength of the El Nino event developing in the tropical Pacific is reported to be "Godzilla-level" in the Guardian, external. It quotes figures from climate scientists who say more than 450,000 people are projected to die from droughts, wildfires or flooding caused by the weather phenomenon in the next six months.The former chairman of John Lewis Sir Charlie Mayfield has told the Times, external that what he calls the "culture of fear" preventing managers from talking to staff if they are off sick, must end. Sir Charlie, who now advises the government, tells the paper he wants to "change the norms" of people emailing or texting their employer if they can't go to work, so both sides feel more able to talk about sickness and develop "return to work plans" together.The Sun, external highlights the former Daily Mirror Editor Piers Morgan's demand for Princess Diana's brother Earl Spencer's book to be withdrawn from sale, because Morgan was wrongly accused in it of being behind the publication of intrusive photos. The main headline is "Pulp fiction."The Daily Mail, external reports research which shows there is a "sweet" spot" when it comes to the vocal pitch that women find attractive. The study, led by a team at Durham University, found that voices which are too high, or too low, lose their appeal. Those judged most attractive were in the "moderate pitch range" and researchers said that was similar to the voices of former US President Barack Obama and the actor Gerard Butler.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Burn to be mild' and 'Pulp fiction'
